Customer onboarding automation: what to automate

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 25, 2026•9 min read

Customer onboarding automation means having software run the account-opening steps of a bank's or fintech's written procedure: collecting identifying information, verifying identity, identifying the beneficial owners of a business, screening, rating risk and recording the result, with a person deciding wherever the procedure requires judgment. Under 31 CFR 1020.220, a bank's identity procedures "must enable the bank to form a reasonable belief that it knows the true identity of each customer." Automated customer onboarding has to meet that standard on every run.

This guide covers the rules, which steps a system can run and which stay with a person, what the procedure and record must say, and how to test. It is about onboarding individuals and businesses at US banks and the fintechs that work with them. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What the rules require at account opening

Identity: the CIP rule

31 CFR 1020.220 requires a written Customer Identification Program "appropriate for the bank's size and type of business". Before opening an account, the bank must obtain at least a name, a date of birth for an individual, an address and an identification number. It must verify identity "within a reasonable time after the account is opened", by documents, non-documentary methods or both. Our guide to KYC checks covers the methods.

Under 2025 orders from the OCC, FDIC and NCUA (June 27) and the Federal Reserve (July 31), with FinCEN's concurrence, a bank may obtain TIN information from a third-party source instead of the customer. The bank "must still obtain the full TIN from a third-party source prior to opening an account", and using the exemption is optional.

Beneficial owners of business customers

For legal entity customers, 31 CFR 1010.230 requires written procedures to identify and verify beneficial owners: each individual who directly or indirectly owns 25 percent or more of the equity interests, and a single individual with significant responsibility to control, manage or direct the entity. Verification procedures must contain, at a minimum, the elements used for individual customers under the CIP rule. FinCEN's exceptive relief order FIN-2026-R001 of February 13, 2026 lets a bank limit this to three cases: when a legal entity customer first opens an account, when the bank knows of facts that "would reasonably call into question the reliability" of the information it holds, and as its ongoing due diligence procedures require. On November 17, 2026, FinCEN issued a proposed rule to strengthen customer due diligence requirements. Until a final rule takes effect, 31 CFR 1010.230 and the order continue to apply.

Customer due diligence

31 CFR 1020.210 requires risk-based procedures for understanding "the nature and purpose of customer relationships for the purpose of developing a customer risk profile", and for ongoing monitoring.

Which onboarding steps to automate and which stay with a person

A system can run most of the collection, matching and recordkeeping; judgment stays with a named reviewer. This table works as an automated onboarding checklist for one run:

StepWhat the system runsWhat a person decidesRule or guidance
1. NoticeShows the customer identification notice before the application is submittedThe notice wording, once1020.220(a)(5)
2. Identifying informationRequires name, date of birth, address and identification number; can fetch the TIN from a third party under the 2025 ordersExceptions the procedure allows, such as a customer who has applied for a TIN1020.220(a)(2)(i)
3. Identity verificationRuns the document or non-documentary check and records the method and resultSubstantive discrepancies, unfamiliar documents, and any customer who cannot be verified1020.220(a)(2)(ii) and (iii)
4. Beneficial ownersCollects the certification, checks that owners at 25 percent or more and one control person are listed, verifies each one, checks whether this is a first accountOwnership information that looks unreliable or does not match other records1010.230; FIN-2026-R001
5. ScreeningScreens the customer and owners against sanctions and other listsWhether a possible match is the same personOFAC regulations (31 CFR chapter V)
6. Risk ratingApplies the bank's rating rules to products, customer type, geography and expected activityHigh ratings and any change or override of a rating1020.210(a)(2)(v)
7. EDD triggersRoutes the file to enhanced due diligence and requests the extra informationThe EDD conclusionFFIEC CDD section
8. Account decisionOpens the account when every check has passed and no rule requires reviewDeclines, restricted use while verification continues, closure, and whether to file a SAR1020.220(a)(2)(iii)
9. RecordWrites the record of what was collected, checked and decidedNothing1020.220(a)(3); 1010.230(i)

The CIP rule has its own government list check, but the FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual notes that, as of its publication date, "no designated government lists for CIP purposes exist". OFAC screening and section 314(a) requests "remain separate and distinct requirements", so the procedure should name them as separate steps. Our guide to reviewing a sanctions hit covers the reviewer's side.

Banks have room to design their risk rating. FinCEN's consolidated CDD FAQs say it is not a requirement that banks "use a specific method or categorization to establish a customer risk profile". The FFIEC manual's CDD section adds that the program should be "sufficiently detailed to distinguish between significant variations" in customer risk.

How to automate customer onboarding, step by step

A practical order for building automated onboarding workflows:

  1. List each step of the written procedure, its data and its rule.
  2. Mark the review points: what sends a file to a person, and which person.
  3. Write the routing as rules a tester can read, such as "any screening hit goes to a reviewer", each tied to a procedure section.
  4. Connect the data sources: the application, the verification vendor, the screening provider and your existing customer records, so a run can tell a first account from a repeat one.
  5. Test on past files before any live customer, then run alongside the current process for a period.
  6. Go live with change control: a new procedure version or vendor change is a release, tested like one.

Verkflo runs this kind of procedure today as a versioned agent that pulls applicant data from Sumsub, screens in ComplyAdvantage and pauses for a reviewer where the procedure says so, as the KYC onboarding review use case shows.

What the written procedure must say

The rules and the FFIEC manual point to what an automated onboarding procedure needs in writing:

  • The identifying information collected, the documents accepted, and the non-documentary methods used, with when each applies (1020.220(a)(2)).
  • What happens when identity cannot be verified: when not to open, the terms under which a customer may use the account while verification continues, when to close it, and when to file a SAR.
  • How beneficial owners are collected, verified and, under the 2026 order, when they are not collected again.
  • Who may change a customer's risk profile. The FFIEC CDD section says procedures "should indicate who in the organization is authorized to change a customer's risk profile."
  • When EDD applies and what it collects. The same section says procedures "should define both when and what additional customer information will be collected", and lists examples such as source of funds and wealth, occupation or type of business, and financial statements for business customers.
  • Standards for documenting the analysis, "including guidance for resolving issues when insufficient or inaccurate information is obtained."

See also KYB and beneficial ownership.

Exceptions and manual review

Common exits are a failed verification, an unlisted document type, an address or date of birth that disagrees between sources, an ownership chart that does not add up, a screening hit, a high rating and an EDD trigger. For each, the procedure should name the reviewer, what they see, their options and the time allowed.

Repeat business customers need their own exit. Under FIN-2026-R001, a bank need not identify and verify owners again when an existing legal entity customer opens another account, unless it knows of facts that call the earlier information into question. When its ongoing due diligence procedures call for it, the bank may rely on earlier information if the customer "certifies or confirms (verbally or in writing)" that it is up to date and accurate. If the customer cannot, the bank must identify and verify the owners again.

What to log for examiners

The CIP rule sets the minimum record: all identifying information obtained, a description of each document relied on, "a description of the methods and the results" of non-documentary checks, and the resolution of each substantive discrepancy. Identifying information is kept for five years after the account is closed, and the other records for five years after they are made. 1010.230(i) sets the same pattern for beneficial ownership, including the certification (see the FFIEC beneficial ownership section). Where ongoing due diligence leads a bank to rely on earlier information, the 2026 order says it "must maintain a record" of the customer's certification or confirmation.

An automated run should also record the procedure version, each rule that routed or passed the file, the reviewer's decision and reason, and the time of each step, so a tester can follow each file. If a vendor does part of the work, the FFIEC manual is clear that "the bank is ultimately responsible for compliance with the requirements of the CIP rule."

How to test before going live

Run the automated procedure on past files with known outcomes: clean individuals, businesses with layered ownership, screening hits and customers who could not be verified. Compare each result with the analyst's decision, then run in parallel with the current process. The December 2018 joint statement on innovative efforts to combat money laundering says "pilot programs in and of themselves should not subject banks to supervisory criticism even if the pilot programs ultimately prove unsuccessful", and also that banks must continue to meet their BSA/AML compliance obligations while they develop them. If a step uses a model to score or decide, read what SR 26-2 changes for model risk too.

What customer onboarding software for banks has to support

Check that the software can hold every step in the table, stop a file at each review point, show the reviewer the evidence, apply the 2026 order's ownership rules with any confirmation recorded, and export a complete record per customer. Our guide to KYC software covers vendor questions, and KYC automation covers the wider set of reviews.

Common questions

What is the onboarding process for banks?

The bank gives notice, collects and verifies identifying information, identifies and verifies beneficial owners of legal entity customers, screens, rates risk, applies EDD where needed, decides and keeps the record. What is KYC? covers the wider program.

What is a customer onboarding process?

The written steps a bank or fintech follows to accept a new customer, from application to account decision. Automating it, sometimes called client onboarding automation, means software runs the steps and routes judgment calls to people.

Can customer onboarding be fully automated?

Clean files can pass without a person if the procedure allows it. Files that cannot be verified, possible screening matches, high ratings and EDD cases still need a reviewer.

Do we need to re-identify beneficial owners for every new account?

Not under FIN-2026-R001, which a bank may use at its discretion. Owners must still be identified and verified at the first account, when the bank knows of facts that call the information into question, and when its ongoing due diligence procedures require it.
